EU AI Act enters force

The European Union's AI Act entered into force this week, beginning a staged rollout that will run until 2028 for the highest-risk systems.

Timeline of obligations

Prohibited practices apply after six months, general-purpose model rules after twelve, and the bulk of high-risk obligations after twenty-four.

Who is affected

Providers placing systems on the EU market are covered regardless of where they are established, as are deployers using outputs inside the Union.

Prohibited practices

Social scoring by public authorities, untargeted scraping of facial images and emotion inference at work are banned outright under the first phase.

General-purpose models

Model providers must publish training-data summaries and respect copyright reservations, with extra duties once a compute threshold is crossed.

High-risk classification

Annex III lists the use cases treated as high risk, including recruitment, credit scoring, education access and critical infrastructure management.

Enforcement and penalties

National market-surveillance authorities lead enforcement, with fines that scale to global turnover for the most serious prohibited-practice breaches.

The AI Office

A central AI Office coordinates general-purpose model supervision and can request documentation directly from providers of the largest models.

Sandboxes for smaller firms

Member states must run regulatory sandboxes so smaller providers can test compliance approaches before a system reaches the open market.

What companies do next

Most legal teams start with an inventory of deployed systems, then map each one to a risk tier before deciding what documentation is missing.

Open questions

Harmonised standards are still being drafted, so the practical bar for conformity assessments remains unclear for several Annex III use cases.
